analysis.one_liner: Gives one drug maker two extra years of exclusive sales rights for an arthritis painkiller.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have handed one drug maker two extra years of monopoly sales on an FDA-approved arthritis drug, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The drug oxaprozin, an arthritis painkiller, spent 21 years in FDA review, so its patent expired around the time it was approved in 1992. This bill would grant its maker a fresh two-year exclusive right to sell it starting in October 1997, blocking generic drug companies from even filing FDA applications in the meantime. It was introduced days before the Christmas recess, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and never acted on before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The maker of oxaprozin (the brand drug Daypro, then sold by Searle) would gain two additional years, from October 1997 to October 1999, of exclusive rights to make, sell, and import the drug, with full patent-style legal protection against infringement [S2][S3]. That means two more years of brand-name prices with no generic competition.

how_it_helps.text: Grants the owner of the rights to oxaprozin a two-year entitlement, beginning October 29, 1997, to exclude others from making, using, selling, or importing the drug's active ingredient, enforced under patent law [S2][S3].
Blocks anyone from submitting an FDA application for a generic version before the exclusivity ends, regardless of purpose, delaying cheaper competition by design [S3].

The bill's stated justification is that FDA review of oxaprozin lasted 21 years — from an initial filing in 1971 to approval on October 29, 1992 — consuming the drug's entire 17-year patent life, and that Congress had previously restored time for other NSAIDs hurt by the same FDA delays [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients, insurers, and anyone buying oxaprozin would pay brand-name prices for two extra years while generic versions were legally kept off the market, including during the period when generic makers are barred from even starting the FDA approval process [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill legally prohibits submission of generic drug applications until the two-year entitlement expires, so consumers face two more years of monopoly pricing on a drug the FDA had already declared safe and effective [S3].

The relief is tailored so narrowly that it fits exactly one drug — approved by the FDA on October 29, 1992, after more than 120 months of review — a form of targeted legislation that grants a commercial benefit to a single company rather than setting a general rule [S2][S3].

An honest supporter would concede the cost side of the trade: whatever the fairness of compensating for FDA delay, the money comes directly out of the pockets of people who need the drug, with no price restraint attached.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's argument — that the maker lost its whole patent to an unusually slow FDA review, and Congress had compensated similar NSAID cases before — is not baseless, and the bill cites a GAO finding of a two-year FDA backlog affecting the whole class [S3]. But the remedy is a straight transfer: two years of monopoly pricing on an already-approved drug, paid by patients and insurers, with no offsetting benefit to them. The narrowly drafted criteria make clear it was written for one product. On the merits, the public cost outweighs the fairness argument for the company.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 21, 1995, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day, and nothing further happened before that Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Simon introduced the bill on December 21, 1995, with Republican Sens. Hatch, Bond, and Ashcroft joining as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S3][S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill, and it never received a floor vote or any other action before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

Because the bill never became law, the two-year exclusivity it would have created beginning October 29, 1997 was never granted, and the maker's exclusive rights ended with the expiration of the original patent [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients and generic drug makers are better off, because the two-year extension of exclusive, patent-protected sales of oxaprozin never became law and cheaper generic competition could enter on schedule. The brand maker lost the chance for two more years of monopoly pricing.

for.name: Sen. Paul Simon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 21, 1995 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan: one Democrat introduced the bill and three Republicans (Hatch, Bond, and Ashcroft) joined as original cosponsors, with no opposition ever recorded because the bill died in committee without a vote [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would grant its maker a fresh two-year monopoly on sales starting October 1997, enforced under patent law, after the drug's original patent had been consumed by FDA review [S2][S3]. The gain comes directly at patients' expense through two more years of brand-name prices.

The bill bars generic companies from submitting FDA applications for oxaprozin before the exclusivity expires, delaying cheaper competing products [S3]. Its interests run with those of consumers who want lower prices.
